context: A box of coloured blocks (purple, orange and white). The total number of blocks is stated, and one block is selected at random.
stem: A box contains {=T} coloured blocks: {=r} are purple, {=o} are orange and {=g} are white. A block is selected at random. What is the probability that the block is purple or white? Give your answer as a decimal.
solution: The total is {=T} blocks, so $P(\text{purple})=\frac{{=r}}{{=T}}$ and $P(\text{white})=\frac{{=g}}{{=T}}$.
A block cannot be both purple and white, so the events are mutually exclusive: $P(\text{purple and white})=0$ and $P(\text{purple or white})=P(\text{purple})+P(\text{white})$.
notes: Entry-point skill: the total is given in the stem, so the student only reads off two single-colour probabilities and adds them (modelled on book 11b and 17e, which also start from a counted collection). T is limited to 10, 20, 25 or 50 so that s/T is an exact decimal of at most two places and no rounding rule is needed; the answer string is formatted by fixed(..., 2) (e.g. 0.60), so a numeric comparison should accept 0.6. Orange is the colour not asked for, and both asked colours are single-colour events that cannot occur together. Constraints are invariants of the draws (r and o are at most T//3+1, so g >= 2 and s <= T-2). No mcq is used, so no misconception ids are attached.
